body.text: In short:
The Coalition says it will not back a pact with Vanuatu because it commits Australia to hit net zero by 2050.
The deal is key to the government's strategic architecture to reinforce Australia’s position and stop China from gaining a military foothold in the Pacific.
What's next?
The move does not threaten the Nakamal Agreement in the short term as the government does not require parliamentary support for ratification.
The federal government has lashed the Coalition after it declared it would not back a sweeping strategic pact with Vanuatu because it commits Australia to hitting net zero by 2050.

The Nakamal Agreement was widely expected to sail through federal parliament without controversy after being signed by Anthony Albanese and Vanuatu's Prime Minister Jotham Napat following months of sometimes tortuous negotiations.

The government sees the hard-won $500 million deal as a key part of the strategic architecture it has built to reinforce Australia's position and stop China from gaining a military foothold in the region — even though some key provisions were watered down to secure Vanuatu's agreement.
A parliamentary committee scrutinising the pact has now recommended parliament ratify the agreement but Coalition parliamentarians have issued a dissenting report.

They've taken aim at a clause which says both countries "recognise the existential threat posed by climate change and commit to transition their economies to net zero by 2050 and meet their respective renewable energy targets".
Australia has legislated a 43 per cent cut in net greenhouse gas emissions from 2005 levels by 2030.
Last year, the government set a 2035 target of a 62–70 per cent cut from 2005 levels, with net zero emissions by 2050.

The Coalition has vowed to ditch net zero if it wins office, and the Coalition committee members say the Nakamal Agreement in its current form unreasonably binds the hands of future Australian governments.

"This is an unacceptable infringement on the principle of popular sovereignty, and is a risk to the Australian economy and people, as governments will be restrained in their ability to change climate and energy policy to rapidly react to changing economic circumstances and technological developments," they write.

They also warn that the climate clause poses an "unacceptable risk" to the broader agreement because "the current government is not on track to reach net zero by 2050 or deliver on its renewable energy targets made binding by the agreement".
"The current agreement is set up for failure," they say.

"A breach of those clauses contained within Article 4 (on climate change) would lead to the invalidation of all other clauses, including those … which Coalition Members consider essential to the security and stability of Australia and the Pacific."
The move does not threaten the Nakamal Agreement in the short term as the government does not require parliamentary support for ratification, and the committee's recommendations are not binding.

But the government has secured bipartisan backing for the other strategic pacts it has landed in the Pacific — including the Falepili Union with Tuvalu, the Nauru Treaty and the Pukpuk Treaty with Papua New Guinea — and fears the schism could undermine Australia's strategic position in the region.
The dissenting report also raises questions about the Nakamal Agreement's durability if there is a change of government in Australia.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong excoriated the Coalition this morning, saying the statement was a "triumph of ideology over national security".
"The same ideological wars that the Coalition … are engaged in to not support an agreement that is so important for Australia's national security," she said.
"Our region is where we build our security, and the Coalition are not up to the job."
A government spokesperson said it was "remarkable that the Liberals and Nationals continue to disrespect Pacific priorities".

"We know that the Albanese government's reliability and credibility with Pacific partners, including on climate change, has enabled us to make transformational breakthroughs like the Nakamal Agreement with Vanuatu," they said.
"In the strategic circumstances we face now, disregarding the existential threat of climate change for the Pacific in this way will make Australia more vulnerable."
It's still possible that both sides of politics find a compromise on the agreement ahead of ratification.

Coalition MPs on the committee say if the government won't amend that section of the Nakamal Agreement it should issue a national interest analysis which clarifies the legal implications of the climate clause should a future government amend or repeal net zero — which could open the way to bipartisan support.

But the federal government is unlikely to agree to this — particularly as it has been planning to wrap up the ratification process by the end of this week, allowing the treaty to enter into force before parliament rises for the long summer break.
The dispute opens up a new political front on major foreign policy issues, alongside the stoush over the EU free trade agreement.
The controversy has also reared its head just before Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale lands in Canberra ahead of signing a sweeping new treaty with Australia on Wednesday.
A large delegation of ministers and MPs from Solomon Islands is expected to accompany Mr Wale for the ceremony.

While the text isn't yet public, the treaty is widely expected to provide Australia with guarantees designed to block China from securing a persistent security presence in the Pacific nation, and to limit Beijing's investment in sensitive infrastructure.

That would be a significant victory for the government and Senator Wong, who in 2022 called the security pact signed by Solomon Islands and China the "worst failure of Australian foreign policy in the Pacific since the end of World War II".
